events.excerpt: Summary As part of regular governance upkeep, Uniswap Labs reviews the protocol infrastructure that governance owns and brings forward improvements as they are needed. This RFC proposes two technical updates: Upgrade the VolatilePair Hook on Ethereum Update the protocol fee releaser on X Layer Below we outline the background and proposed changes for both initiatives. Part 1: VolatilePair Hook Upgrade Background VolatilePair Hook is a Uniswap v4 dynamic-fee hook built by Uniswap Labs. It went live on Ethereum on October 14 with the ETH/USDC pool and has since launched on Robinhood Chain (ETH/USDG). Volatile pairs did more than $500 billion in volume on Uniswap this year. In a static-fee pool, when the price moves elsewhere, LPs end up absorbing the cost while the pool quotes a stale price and someone else trades against it to keep the difference. VolatilePair Hook prices both sides of the trade, setting separate buy and sell fees on every swap: When the pool price rises, buying costs more and selling costs less. When pool price falls, the fees flip. After a large price move, trades that push the price back pay a temporary fee . events.excerpt: This is fascinating : The video describes a technique that can reveal where an otherwise unidentifiable recording was made by analyzing its audio for the faint sounds of passing aircraft. The technique is both fascinating and frightening. It works by looking at Doppler curves, which plot the way a plane’s sound changes as it passes overhead because of the Doppler effect. This is the same familiar Doppler effect that causes the frequency of a siren to rise as it approaches and then fall as it passes by and moves away. More generally, it’s the phenomenon whereby the frequency of a wave perceived by an observer changes when the observer and the source of the wave are moving in relation to one another. […] It’s sound that’s relevant here, though, and specifically the sound of aeroplanes. Early in his video, Colsto brings up a map of the flights that were in the air at the time the video he’s tracing was recorded. Much of this information is publicly available. Aircraft equipped with Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast (ADS-B) transmit data about their position, velocity, and altitude, which flight-tracking services collect and make available to the public. While not every plane is tracked, the system provides an enormous amount of information about aircraft movements.
events.headline: Pinpointing Location of Videos from Background Airplane Sounds

events.excerpt: The highest priorities for the transition to post-quantum cryptography are the basic building blocks of authenticated key-agreement protocols such as TLS. Without these building blocks in place, secure communication on the Internet will not be possible once cryptographically relevant quantum computers come online. However, today we rely on quantum-vulnerable cryptography for much more than TLS. Privacy Pass is a protocol used by site operators like Cloudflare to help protect applications from abuse. One way we do this is by rate limiting individual clients so that no one client consumes too many of the site's resources. Normally this involves some combination of friction or loss of privacy for users: CAPTCHAs or other challenges to moderate traffic, along with accounts and fingerprinting to identify traffic.Privacy Pass was designed to avoid this tradeoff between friction and privacy. The basic idea is that a client gets issued a number of tokens , which they can redeem in exchange for access to the site. Crucially, each token is unlinkable to the client it was issued to, ensuring the client can use the site as they always had without sacrificing privacy. events.excerpt: Daniil Ankushin, Nethermind. Verify-budget figures: method by Daniil Ankushin, benchmark and measurements by Manuel Arto. On frame transactions a shielded pool pays its own gas, so a private withdrawal needs no relayer. We ran a real BN254 Groth16 pool this way on current Nethermind master: a withdrawal costs 679,322 gas. With EIP-8250 nonce keys, many withdrawals can come from the one pool address at once. Two things do not work yet. The proof check is over the spec cap on validation gas, and a pool cannot pay for a call from the user’s own address. The pool we ran is soispoke’s minimal-shielded-pool ( GitHub - soispoke/minimal-shielded-pool · GitHub ). How a withdrawal works In a withdrawal the pool is the sender. Its VERIFY code checks the zk proof and approves execution and payment. The user needs no funded account and does not appear in the transaction. Two drafts make this safe in a public mempool. With EIP-8250 the pool uses the note’s nullifiers as nonce keys. Each withdrawal has its own nonce key, so withdrawals with the pool as sender do not compete for one nonce. A side effect: a nullifier that was already used is a used nonce key, so the protocol refuses a double spend before the pool’s code runs. events.excerpt: Last week’s security notice on the Fearless Wallet browser extension ( notice ) says that from February 2025, unlocking the wallet sent your private key to a server run by the attacker. The notice links a write-up that walks through the code at fixed commits ( write-up ). I read it and then went through the repo history myself. None of it was hidden. It sat in public source the whole time. I audit smart contracts, not browser extensions, but the review lessons carry over to any code that touches keys. Like the write-up, I’m sticking to what the code and the history show, not who wrote it or why. How it got in, and how it left The code arrived in PR #1022 of soramitsu/fearless-wallet-web, titled “Ton Service”. It was open for ten weeks and merged on 19 February 2025 as one squashed commit, “TON ecosystem”: 251 files, 4,690 lines added and 6,119 removed. The PR has no review comments. The function that matters is about 25 lines, in a new 180 line file, inside a diff of almost 11,000 changed lines whose title says it adds TON. It left the same way. The code was deleted from the source on 25 June 2026, inside a release commit with about 80,000 changed lines. What each piece looked like in a diff The name. events.excerpt: Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running. Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post , we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage. We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the ref

events.excerpt: AI agents do more than generate answers. They search for information, query databases, write and test code and take action. Each of those steps relies on a CPU, with agents moving between GPU reasoning and CPU execution throughout a task. As businesses put more agents to work, AI factories need CPUs that can execute those steps quickly and support many agents at once, all within the limits of available power. What this means: AI infrastructure providers need to support more agents without making each one wait longer to get work done. And critically, AI factories are power limited. This means operators need to choose infrastructure that maximizes the work done for every watt. Why it matters: NVIDIA Vera delivers both fast agent performance and high capacity per watt within a single CPU. That gives providers one CPU for a range of agent workloads, rather than having to mix and match fast and dense x86 parts to balance speed and capacity. The data that proves it: In a 100-megawatt data center comparison, NVIDIA found that a single Vera CPU performs better than the fastest x86 CPU and the most energy-efficient x86 CPU. Vera delivers industry-leading agent speed while enabling 1.6x more agents per watt versus the fastest x86 CPU. Vera delivers 2x faster agent speed with leading energy
events.headline: Vera Delivers the Best of Both Worlds: Highest Throughput and Fastest Agents

events.excerpt: AI Agents now act on the web for millions of people. To a Site, an Agent can take many forms. It may be indistinguishable from a human user carrying out a task, or it might look like one visitor carrying many Users. This removes the ability for the Site to recognize, serve, and hold accountable the user or users behind the Agent, and causes the Site to face the costs when something goes wrong. This post argues that in order for Sites to maximize the access they provide to Agents, the ecosystem must develop new mechanisms to preserve the relationship between Sites and Users. Traditionally, in Security and Fraud Prevention, that requires three things: Identity, Reputation, and Accountability, allowing Sites to answer: Is the person acting being truthful about who they are? Is that person trustworthy? And who answers for the action? “Personal AI Agents” (“Agents” for short) are automations that take instructions from a human (“User”) and pursue a goal by controlling a cloud computer or browser. They are usually hosted and maintained by an “Operator” as part of a managed service or consumer offering. Examples include Muse from Meta and dots from OpenAI, and more are launching all the time. events.excerpt: Hi all. We recently opened a discussion in the Solana SIMD repository about a new class of smart contracts we’re loosely calling “inference programs,” or “Actually Smart Contracts.” We’d value technical input from this community on whether a similar proposal could be feasible on Ethereum, before we write anything for it. The idea, briefly: a contract stores a prompt and the rules that shape it (a DAO constitution, a policy, a standard). Another contract asks it a question with evidence. AI models from different operators answer off chain, each signs a vote, and the caller checks the signed result before acting. The motivator was Anthropic’s recent work on zero-knowledge proofs of LLM inference . events.excerpt: Walraswap: equilibrium-based decentralized exchange integrating external AMM liquidity This is an announcement of the research article with the same title and a brief informal intro for ethresear.ch. A classic approach to tackling MEV in decentralized exchanges on Ethereum is to enable a mechanism that receives trade orders during a block interval and settles all the swaps in a batch following a fairness criterion. It is an old problem. I imagine that an informed reader might feel somewhat skeptical. Thoughts of this kind were expressed in 2014 in this Reddit post . CoW Swap, UniswapX, 1inch’s Fusion, Sorella’s Angstrom, and Propellerheads’ Turbine have all tackled the problem using batch trading in one way or another. Walraswap started in 2023 at Flashbots, independently of the previous and closely related work by Ramseyer, Goyal, Goel, and Mazières: Augmenting Batch Exchanges… and SPEEDEX . The central feature in common: we treat the DEX problem from the point of view of the theory of equilibrium for an exchange economy with n tokens. events.excerpt: At a glance Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here. Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for. PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach. We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and nev
events.headline: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit

events.excerpt: Larger models, longer contexts and agentic applications are increasing GPU memory pressure while supply tightens and prices rise — a trend expected to continue through the near term. NVIDIA works closely with memory partners to rapidly adopt the latest memory technologies. NVIDIA was first to adopt HBM3e and HBM4 technologies into an accelerated computing stack. But the approach isn’t to simply pack more memory onto the GPU. It’s full-stack codesign. NVIDIA intentionally designs GPUs, CPUs, networking, storage and software together to get more useful work out of memory at every layer of the AI factory. That matters because an AI factory runs on a memory and storage hierarchy. GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is the fastest, most expensive and most contested tier — with model weights and KV cache competing for limited capacity. Below it sit CPU memory, local SSDs and shared storage, each trading speed for more capacity at a lower cost per bit. How much useful work a byte does depends on how well the whole hierarchy is used: shrinking what must be stored, placing it on the right tier and bringing it back to the GPU before it’s needed. Byte for byte, NVIDIA makes the most efficient use of memory at every layer — and the results show it. From NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra to the Vera Rubin p
events.headline: More Performance From Every Byte: How Full-Stack Codesign Solves AI’s Memory Challenge

events.excerpt: Accessibility work often lives in issue trackers, contribution guidelines, audit reports, team knowledge, and conversations with users. When that information has no predictable home, people who encounter a barrier must search for it, and maintainers lose context as contributors and project ownership change. An ACCESSIBILITY.md file, now visible on repository overview pages, gives a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers. GitHub makes accessibility statements easier to find GitHub now recognizes the ACCESSIBILITY.md file in the repository’s root, .github/ directory, or docs/ directory. A repository can also inherit a statement from its organization’s .github/ repository. For public repositories, maintainers can add or propose a statement from Insights > Community Standards using a concise starter document. GitHub’s community health files help people understand how a project works: Contribution guidelines explain how to propose changes Codes of conduct establish expectations for participation Security policies explain how to report vulnerabilities Recognizing ACCESSIBILITY.md gives accessibility information a dedicated place alongside that guidance. events.excerpt: Abstract This standard defines a proxy that coordinates execution sessions by temporarily caching a program and its associated calldata in transient storage. The proxy forwards the cached program to a fixed implementation through DELEGATECALL and uses a handler flag to control whether subsequent reentrant invocations are dispatched. The program remains unchanged throughout an execution session, while the cached calldata is replaced on each accepted invocation. This enables a single implementation to coordinate callback-driven execution using different programs and calldata without deploying a new contract for each execution. Motivation Many advanced execution strategies require dynamically changing execution logic, particularly when interacting with external contracts that invoke callbacks during execution. Traditionally, dynamically changing the execution logic of a contract may require deploying a new contract containing the desired runtime code. This introduces deployment costs, including contract creation and code-deposit costs. Flash Loan Proxy separates the execution program from the implementation responsible for interpreting it. Instead of deploying a new contract for each program, callers provide the program as calldata. The proxy temporarily caches the program and forwa

events.excerpt: Proposal Type : Ratification Executive Summary This Ratification vote adds an Upgrade Authority Transfer policy to the Governing Policies section of the Standard Rollup Charter. It sets out how a Chain Governor may request that upgrade authority for its chain be transferred from the Security Council to an address of its choosing, so the chain can manage upgrades itself or through a third party. Under the policy, the Optimism Foundation confirms a valid request and publishes a public notice on the Governance Forum. After a mandatory 30-day notice period, the Security Council is directed to execute the transfer. Once the transfer is executed, the chain ceases to be a Standard Rollup. This is a non-fork upgrade. It changes Charter language only: no smart contract or node software changes are required, and this proposal executes no onchain transactions. Motivation The Standard Rollup Charter defines how a chain becomes a Standard Rollup, including authorizing the Security Council to perform upgrades. It does not define how a chain leaves. Today, a Chain Governor that wants to take back upgrade authority has no published path, and any transfer would require ad hoc governance action. This gap matters for three reasons: Predictability for Chain Governors. Handing upgrade authority to th

events.excerpt: Important Optional but highly recommended upgrade. v2.5.1 is a hardening & maintenance release. No protocol fork is activated, and operators can upgrade in-place. v2.5.1 carries robustness improvements across the P2P layer, block processing, the transaction pool and the public/admin APIs, together with a handful of API and SDK fixes. Most changes are internal; the user-visible ones are listed below. What's Changed Hardening & Robustness These changes tighten resource bounds and failure handling throughout the node. They do not change consensus rules: every bound is sized above what a valid block can hold under the current 40M block gas limit. Networking : new blocks received from a peer are handed off through a per-peer mailbox instead of being processed on the peer's read loop. Transaction broadcast now uses a single bounded queue and writer per peer. Future-block cache entries are capped per peer and bound to their header. Inbound connection attempts are rate-limited per source (one per 30s for a non-LAN IPv4 address or IPv6 /64 prefix), matching go-ethereum ( #1699 ). Internal consistency fixes in the discv5 topic table. Block decoding : stricter bounds while decoding block headers and bodies (header field widths, total clause count per block). events.excerpt: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016. The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President ( AS2650 ). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period. The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica , a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications .
